Industry News: Intel One Mono font (2023)

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.
  • It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.
  • It has been revealed that identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Introducing Intel One Mono, an expressive monospaced font family that’s built with clarity, legibility, and the needs of developers in mind.

It’s easier to read, and available for free, with an open-source font license.

It has been revealed that identifying the typographically underserved low-vision developer audience, Frere-Jones Type designed the Intel One Mono typeface in partnership with the Intel Brand Team and VMLY&R, for maximum legibility to address developers' fatigue and eyestrain and reduce coding errors. A panel of low-vision and legally blind developers provided feedback at each stage of design.

Intel One Mono also covers a wide range of over 200 languages using the Latin script. The Intel One Mono fonts are provided in four weights — Light, Regular, Medium, and Bold — with matching italics, and we are happy to share both an official release of fonts ready to use as well as editable sources.

In a recent development, to install the fonts, please use the provided builds under Releases. Please refer to your software’s documentation for how to activate and use these fonts.

Recent findings suggest that we recommend using these fonts at 7 points and larger in print, 9 pixels and larger on screen. The .ttf, .woff and .woff2 fonts provided in the official release have been manually optimized for screen display, improving clarity and legibility, especially on Windows platforms.

Outside of the default characters, there are a few extra features that are accessible in some applications, as well as via CSS:.

Industry observers note that programming ligatures are not active by default. To use them, activate the stylistic sets of your preference in your code editor. For example:.

You will find editable sources in the sources directory. The instances subfolder contains separate source files for each style of the typeface. Sources are provided in .ufo files, which contain complete artwork, links to OpenType features provided in separate .fea files, as well as meta information like naming and vertical alignments for each style of the typeface.

These are not installable fonts, but rather the source files that produce them: UFO (Unified Font Object) is an open, human-readable font source file format; you can find the file spec here. These sources were created using RoboFont. Many other font editors will also be able to open .ufo files; we recommend using RoboFont version 4.4.

For instances, you will find postscript and truetype subfolders; these contain separate source files for the .otf format and the .ttf/.woff/.woff2 files respectively. Since the format for the outline drawings differs between these sets of formats, for best results we recommend using the postscript sources to create .otf fonts, and the TrueType sources to create .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 fonts.

After making your desired edits, you can generate installable fonts directly from the font editor using its “Generate Font” functionality. If you use RoboFont, any install options should default to the ideal settings, but here they are for reference:.

Sources indicate that if you would like to apply edits across multiple weights, a more advanced yet potentially efficient way is to edit the masters. These are special sources that describe the extreme points in the design space — the lightest and heaviest weights for both roman and italic designs.

After editing masters, you will need to rerun interpolation to generate individual weights and styles within that design space. This requires the .designspace files enclosed with the masters. The designspace format is an open, XML-based format that describes interpolation spaces (format specification for reference). For a RoboFont-based workflow we recommend Skateboard for interpolation; you can also use the free DesignSpaceEditor extension to view and edit these files.

Note that masters are only available in postscript format, so they will be best for creating .otf fonts. If you need to make TrueType based builds from the masters, we recommend QuadraticConverter for best quality conversion of the curves before generating .ttf, .woff, or .woff2 files; mind that the results will not match the provided instances precisely.

According to recent reports, NB: The prepared instances contain some additional data that cannot be maintained through interpolation. For best results, compare upcoming interpolations to the existing instance sources and upgrade them accordingly, specifically the information accessible through the Font Info panels.

Sources indicate that for TrueType-based formats (.ttf, .woff, .woff2 files), the official releases are manually optimized for screen rendering. These “hinting” sources are stored separately from the .ufo files, which do not contain any TrueType hinting information. When rebuilding TrueType-based formats, we recommend using the “autohint” option to achieve reasonable, though not identical screen rendering.

If you would like to access and edit manual hinting instructions, you will find these in the separate set of source files under hinting/truetype hinting source. These special TTF files will be viewable and editable using Microsoft VTT.

If you have requests for edits or additions to the official releases, please open complications and we will try to accomodate them.

TDK will spend $635M to double sensor output for robots and AI data centres

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • The company plans to double output of its TMR sensors by 2031.
  • Japan’s TDK aims to invest $635M to double output of its tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) sensors by 2031, Bloomberg reported.
  • Japan’s TDK aims to invest $635M to double its output of high-end magnetic sensors by 2031, as demand grows from cars, humanoid robots and AI data centres, Bloomberg reported.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A TDK factory in Nikaho, Japan. The company plans to double output of its TMR sensors by 2031.

Japan’s TDK aims to invest $635M to double output of its tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) sensors by 2031, Bloomberg reported. The sensors, used in iPhones, are now in demand for cars, humanoid robots and AI data centres, and TDK estimates it makes 80% of the world’s supply.

Japan’s TDK aims to invest $635M to double its output of high-end magnetic sensors by 2031, as demand grows from cars, humanoid robots and AI data centres, Bloomberg reported.

Recent findings suggest that the parts, known as tunnel magnetoresistance (TMR) sensors, are precise and use little power. Apple’s iPhones use them for features like camera stabilisation. TDK estimates it makes 80% of the world’s supply.

Takao Tsutsui, who runs TDK’s sensor unit, mentioned demand is already stretching capacity. He added that TDK could invest more if growth speeds up.

Sources indicate that “We’ve now passed a tipping point. We now see significant demand ahead,” Tsutsui told Bloomberg.

Each humanoid robot uses dozens of TMR sensors, a TDK spokesperson mentioned. Chinese firms, which build almost every humanoid shipped today, are already retooling phone factories to make more. In data centres, the sensors help adjust power flows as computing loads change and watch over liquid-cooling systems.

Sources indicate that TDK, which made its name with cassette tapes, has largely missed out on the AI boom so far. Rivals Murata and Taiyo Yuden have done better, as AI servers soak up so many parts that carmakers face capacitor shortages. TDK’s shares have given up all their gains this year.

It has been revealed that the extra output will come from a latest plant in Niigata prefecture, which TDK said in June would open in 2029. Customers asked TDK to make sensors outside its existing plant in Nagano, as it is often their only supplier.

“We almost always end up being the sole supplier of TMR sensors,” Tsutsui noted.

Sources indicate that others are chasing the same market. Germany’s Infineon is expanding into magnetic sensors, and Bosch is giving its chip and sensor business its own division.

Recent findings suggest that the Siena didn't have an easy ride into our best mattress guide. To be crowned the best cheap mattress we've put it through our rigorous lab-based mattress testing methodology as well as subjecting it to an extended 10 month at-home testing period.

Industry observers note that during that time the Siena continuously impressed with its full-body support. One of the best firm mattresses you can buy online, it holds the spine lifted and aligned, reducing back pain for stomach and back sleepers.

It has been revealed that as someone with a tendency to hunch over my laptop, I need a mattress that helps take strain off my spine. The Siena delivered, as the firm foams held me straight from neck to tailbone, allowing my muscles to unwind.

Industry observers note that the motion isolation is also excellent, as the dense foams stop movement from traveling across the bed. When someone jumped in on one side of the mattress, I could hardly feel them on the other.

Industry News: Major developers, legal experts, and 32 states back Epic in Apple’s SCOTUS appeal

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (870 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that in a significant development in Apple’s Supreme Court appeal of a civil contempt ruling, Epic Games has received backing from 32 states and the District of Columbia, along with major developers, legal experts, former federal judges, and more.
  • Apple’s ever-sprawling fight against Epic Games over its App Store policies is currently being fought on two fronts: in the Supreme Court, where Apple is seeking to overturn a civil contempt ruling, and in the district court, where the companies are disputing what commission, if any, Apple can charge on purchases made through external payment systems.
  • The civil contempt ruling came after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple had violated an earlier injunction issued in its App Store dispute with Epic.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that in a significant development in Apple’s Supreme Court appeal of a civil contempt ruling, Epic Games has received backing from 32 states and the District of Columbia, along with major developers, legal experts, former federal judges, and more. Here are the details.

Apple’s ever-sprawling fight against Epic Games over its App Store policies is currently being fought on two fronts: in the Supreme Court, where Apple is seeking to overturn a civil contempt ruling, and in the district court, where the companies are disputing what commission, if any, Apple can charge on purchases made through external payment systems.

The civil contempt ruling came after Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers found that Apple had violated an earlier injunction issued in its App Store dispute with Epic.

In a nutshell, after she ordered Apple to allow developers to direct people to alternative payment methods outside the App Store, the company responded by allowing external payment links, but imposed a commission of up to 27% on purchases made through them.

Since then, Apple has been trying to overturn the civil contempt ruling, basically arguing that the original injunction did not explicitly prohibit the commissions and other restrictions it imposed on external purchases.

After the Ninth Circuit upheld the contempt finding and denied its request for rehearing, Apple took the case to the Supreme Court, which agreed to hear its appeal.

Importantly, the Supreme Court will only consider the legal standard used to uphold Apple’s civil contempt ruling, not the separate question of what commission, if any, the organization can charge on purchases made through external payment methods.

That will still be determined in the district court, where proceedings have continued despite Apple’s attempts to put them on hold pending the Supreme Court’s decision.

With oral arguments scheduled for January 11, 2027, the case has recently seen a flurry of activity, including Apple’s opening brief in September and Epic’s response earlier this month.

Apple also received support from several organizations in September, including the Washington Legal Foundation, the International Center for Law and Economics, the Computer & Communications Industry Association, and the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. The US government also submitted a brief supporting neither party, arguing that the contempt finding was unjustified over Apple’s 27% commission, but warranted over its restrictions on button designs.

Which brings us to the latest developments: a series of amicus briefs filed in support of Epic Games.

Last week, a total of 9 amicus briefs were filed in support of Epic Games, including one led by Utah and joined by 31 other states and the District of Columbia.

This particular brief notes that “the district court correctly held Apple in contempt for continuing to engage in anticompetitive conduct barred by a prior injunction,” adding:.

According to recent reports, “The court found that Apple engaged in unlawful anti-steering restrictions and required Apple to lift those restrictions. Apple then lifted them in name only, imposed fresh (and substantially similar) strictures on developers that mirrored the old ones and produced the same result. Worse still, Apple did all this in bad faith: Apple knew its behavior was wrong and actively hid that fact from the court, including by providing false testimony. Under any reasonable reading of the district court’s injunction, Apple’s conduct is worthy of civil contempt.”.

The states also argue that “Injunctions in competition cases cannot afford complete relief without addressing the ongoing effects of anticompetitive behavior,” and that “[c]onstruing competition injunctions narrowly defeats their purpose and prevents meaningful redress.”.

Similar arguments appear throughout the other briefs, which include submissions from Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft, as well as nonprofit organizations such as the American Antitrust Institute (AAI), Public Knowledge, and the Electronic Frontier Foundation (EFF).

In their joint brief, Spotify, Match Group, and Microsoft argue that they “have first-hand experience with the effects of Apple’s conduct and evasion efforts,” adding that “Apple’s latest restrictions were no different from the unlawful rules they replaced.”.

According to recent reports, as for the brief filed by former federal judges, they warned that “[i]n cases like these, where enjoined parties seek to circumvent an injunction through reliance on its literal text, courts must have the power of contempt to deter and remedy evasion. Otherwise, courts would be forced into a game of whack-a-mole, trying to anticipate every possible means of evading an injunction […]”.

Arguments by the Little Tech Association, AAI, Public Knowledge, and the EFF all follow a similar line, with some also addressing how Apple’s restrictions on external payment links could affect consumer choice, pricing, and competition.

Here’s the full list of parties that filed amicus briefs in support of Epic Games:.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that password management platform 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker gained access to internal systems and stole select customer account information.
  • 1Password today published a blog post explaining that an attacker “copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset” of its customers, “including the names and email addresses” they use to sign into the platform.
  • In a recent development, according to the tech giant, the incident began on November 19, when it started investigating indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that password management platform 1Password today disclosed a security incident in which an attacker gained access to internal systems and stole select customer account information. Here are the details.

1Password today published a blog post explaining that an attacker “copied a limited amount of customer account information from a subset” of its customers, “including the names and email addresses” they use to sign into the platform.

In a recent development, according to the tech giant, the incident began on November 19, when it started investigating indications that an attacker had gained access to an employee’s corporate GitHub account. The attacker then used that account to access source code and push malicious code to backend services, allowing customer account information to be downloaded.

The manufacturer noted that customer vaults were not affected, adding that all vault contents remain secure:.

Although 1Password did not disclose how many customers were affected, saying only that the breach involved “a subset of our owners,” it did specify what information was compromised, including:.

However, 1Password clarified that the exposed invitation and recovery tokens cannot be used to access accounts on their own, as they also require either an SSO sign-in or a verification code sent to the user’s registered email address.

That remarked, the company confirmed that “the attacker also copied source code from private repositories and gained access” to its CI/CD system, which is essentially its DevOps infrastructure used to build, test, and deploy software.

On that point, 1Password noted that its CI/CD system contains “infrastructure related secrets,” and that it has already rotated or revoked all internal credentials that may have been exposed.

The manufacturer also listed other steps it took in response to the incident, including deactivating the compromised GitHub account, tightening internal security controls, and strengthening the verification codes used in account invitations and recovery emails.

Sources indicate that finally, 1Password mentioned owners do not need to make any changes to their accounts. Still, it recommended that they remain vigilant against phishing attempts, as attackers can use stolen account information to craft convincing emails, messages, or calls that appear legitimate, particularly those involving account invitations or recovery requests.

To learn more about 1Password’s security incident, follow this link.

#143807. Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 24m • 📚 Deep Dive (4718 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Ieee ↗ Open Full Page

Why a Computer Scientist Thinks Superintelligence Won’t Happen

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 24 min read (4718 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Ieee

⏱️ ~24 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction.
  • These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI).
  • These ideas have prompted varied reactions.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Yet trying for it may still be disastrous.

Many people were caught off guard this past summer when employees of one of the world’s leading AI companies began casually debating whether their products would lead to human extinction. It started when Anthropic researcher Jacob Coxon confirmed his resignation, warning that his employer and OpenAI were “racing straight to self-improving superintelligence and gambling with our lives.” Evan Hubinger, Anthropic’s head of alignment science, replied, “Jacob is correct here—we really do earnestly believe AI could kill all humans!” And Anthropic CEO Dario Amodei subsequently told CNN, “I agree with Jacob much more than I disagree with him.”.

These concerns stem from a belief that has circulated in futurist circles for many decades: Once engineers design an AI system capable of improving itself, it will trigger an accelerating cycle of autonomous upgrades known as recursive self-improvement (RSI). The result will be artificial superintelligence (ASI), a system with cognitive capabilities so vastly exceeding those of humans that it will easily evade our control and perhaps even wipe out our species. Artificial superintelligence is, it should be noted, a far more ambitious goal than artificial general intelligence (AGI), which generally refers to AI that can match human capabilities across a broad range of cognitive tasks.

These ideas have prompted varied reactions. Some argue that the concept of ASI is being used for marketing or to instigate regulation that will help the incumbent labs squash new competitors. Others focus on the plausibility of such systems killing us all, debating the finer points of specific scenarios such as AI-engineered superviruses. Still others claim that aligning ASI to human interests is feasible and so we should rush ahead to usher in this digital utopia.

Amid these conversations, one question has received comparatively little attention: From an engineering perspective, is superintelligence even possible? The answer is key because it can help us calibrate our anxieties and develop the most effective possible responses to this emerging technology.

Industry observers note that I recently explored this topic in a computer science doctoral seminar that I taught at Georgetown University, in Washington, D.C., in which my students and I examined the technical and cultural roots of the superintelligence story. (For those who are interested, we published an annotated bibliography of our class readings.) I came away with several key objections to the feasibility of ASI, which I’ll detail below, as well as a deeper fear that even if the promised intelligence explosion never arrives, pursuing it can still create real harm.

RSI is an old concept. In a 1965 paper, statistician I.J. Good speculated that a rapid cycle of AI self-improvement could lead to an “intelligence explosion.” The idea gained traction in the 1990s among the Extropians, a Bay Area futurist group, where it offered a way to discuss ASI without having to address the engineering details of how one would build such a system. The concept was taken up by such notable figures as Eliezer Yudkowsky (who later founded the rationalism movement) and Nick Bostrom (who helped steer effective altruism to focus more on existential risks to humanity).

Recently, however, this topic has shifted from thought experiment to practical engineering within both Anthropic (makers of Claude) and OpenAI (makers of ChatGPT). In a June blog post titled “When AI Builds Itself,” Anthropic described how LLM-powered agents are speeding up the writing, debugging, and optimization of code, and also automating parts of research such as running experiments and logging results. The company’s internal data, the report concluded, “is showing that AI is already accelerating the development of AI systems.” OpenAI has been similarly explicit about its intentions; in a September report, the company confirmed a goal of developing an automated researcher by March 2028.

Recent findings suggest that but do these efforts put the companies on a trajectory toward uncontrollable RSI? Several obstacles undermine this claim. Consider the availability of the data needed to improve AI systems. Through 2023, major advances in LLMs came from scaling up the size of the models. The original GPT-1 had 117 million parameters (values learned during training that shape how the neural network processes information). This quantity jumped to 1.5 billion for GPT-2, to 175 billion for GPT-3, to (likely) more than a trillion for GPT-4’s release three years ago. After GPT-4, however, continued scaling began yielding diminishing returns. This led engineers to increasingly turn their attention toward “post-training” phases, where techniques from reinforcement learning are applied to improve an already trained model’s performance on specific tasks. This approach rewards a model for producing successful responses, helping it better produce similar answers in the future. It requires, however, lots of examples of relevant inputs paired with correct outputs.

It has been revealed that such datasets are relatively easy to generate in highly structured fields such as computer programming and mathematics, which helps explain why we’ve seen rapid and impressive advances in these narrow domains. Progress in areas that lack easy access to this type of training data has been less dramatic. This might explain why AI can tackle advanced theorems but struggles to empty an email inbox. “What if the jagged frontier is mainly math + code (which you can push arbitrarily far with [reinforcement learning techniques]),” the French AI researcher François Chollet recently hypothesized, “and everything else starts to plateau because it is still bottlenecked by human generated data?” The deployment of automated coding agents and LLM-powered researchers won’t overcome this fundamental limitation.

Vernor Vinge1993Proposes that an intelligent machine could design an even smarter one, setting off a potential “intelligence explosion.”REALITY CHECK Notes that faster thinking alone isn’t enough for superintelligence: A ­faster-thinking dog still couldn’t play chess.5. Reality check 2020sFrançois Chollet questions whether LLMs’ current advances in math and coding will extend to domains where training data and reliable feedback are harder to obtain.YOU ARE HERE2026AI systems are already accelerating AI development, and labs are working on automated researchers. But will this lead to an intelligence explosion?THREE POSSIBLE FUTURES1. The Intelligence ExplosionAI systems improve themselves at accelerating speed, surpass human intelligence, and potentially escape our control.2. Danger Without SuperintelligenceThe intelligence explosion never arrives, but increasingly autonomous AI systems cause real-world harm through misuse, poor design, or loss of human control.3. A Useful AI FuturePowerful, specialized AI tools bring major benefits, with constraints that make their behavior easier to predict and control.Claims that RSI is imminent also understate the massive scientific efforts required for major AI advances. Consider the critical role of backpropagation, an algorithm that enables very large neural networks to learn by tuning internal parameters, layer by layer, to reduce errors in their predictions. This algorithm enabled the deep learning revolution, but it didn’t emerge ex nihilo in the minds of its creators. The influential 1986 paper on backpropagation by David Rumelhart, Geoffrey Hinton, and Ronald Williams built on decades of critical breakthroughs in mathematics and computer science.An intelligence explosion leading to ASI would similarly depend on a long sequence of innovations of comparable importance, which would build on many significant science and engineering advances that haven’t yet happened. This would require AI agents to somehow simulate, organize, and evaluate decades of worldwide scientific effort across numerous fields—an impossibly ambitious task. Indeed, recent research led by computer scientists at Princeton found that current AI tools had difficulty making autonomous progress even on highly constrained research questions. “Our results provide early evidence that today’s agents can do the engineering of AI research,” the researchers conclude, “but struggle with critical parts of the research life cycle.” The leap from this current reality to a future in which these same types of tools are automating science is almost too massive to imagine.Finally, the RSI narrative downplays resource limitations. Tens of thousands of human brains have worked for decades, aided by increasingly powerful computers, to develop today’s AI systems, which can match human intelligence in some domains. That represents a massive investment in computation of both the biological and digital variety. What if the next intelligence level requires double the resources, and then the next level requires double again? Soon there would be no number of chips or data centers that we could build to provide the necessary compute and keep advancing toward ASI.Pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.Objection #2: Superintelligence Might Not Be ComputableThere’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.But this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.We cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.At the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s important to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.Penny Gray PhotographyObjection #3: Alignment Isn’t Hard (Given the Right System Design)Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky quickly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.” Explore the Superintelligence Debate In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. It has been revealed that pulling together these threads, I believe that the idea of RSI leading to an intelligence explosion is highly speculative and based on many unproven assumptions. While RSI isn’t definitively impossible, the idea demands more technical skepticism than it’s right now receiving. Carl Sagan’s adage that extraordinary claims require extraordinary evidence certainly applies here.

There’s an implicit claim in the superintelligence discourse that computers are theoretically capable of any calculation that can be imagined, so long as you can find a sufficiently smart algorithm, running on sufficiently powerful digital processors. In this context, RSI is merely a process for rapidly uncovering the special algorithms that can implement unimaginable smarts.

We cannot simply assume that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve.

Industry observers note that but this is not how computer scientists think about computation. In his canonical 1937 paper, “On Computable Numbers,” Alan Turing proved a surprising and relevant result: Most problems cannot be solved by algorithms. His elegant proof established the space of possible problems to be uncountably infinite (like infinite precision decimal numbers), while the space of possible algorithms is only countably infinite (like whole numbers). Later breakthroughs in computational complexity theory established that of the problems that are technically solvable by computers, many would require an astronomically large amount of time and resources to crack, making them practically impossible to solve. Theoretical computer scientists, in other words, don’t assume that computers will solve everything; we’re instead excited whenever we find something that these machines happen to be able to efficiently handle.

It has been revealed that we cannot simply assume, as the futurists often do, that any science fiction scenario we conjure about powerful AI is possible if we give machines enough time to self-improve. There might be some capabilities in which machines can obtain seemingly magical levels of performance, but there will also be many others that no machine, whether computer or human, will ever make much progress.

Recent findings suggest that A relevant counterargument here emphasizes the speed of silicon chips compared to human neurons: Perhaps the sheer speed of digital computation can yield machines that run cognitive circles around our clunky brains, even if they’re not solving vastly more complicated problems than we’re already capable of tackling. But as the computer scientist and science fiction author Vernor Vinge pointed out, rapidity in cognition is not the same as intelligence. Speeding up the mind of a dog, he argued, wouldn’t enable the animal to play chess. Implementing roughly human-level intelligence on a faster machine might be impressive, but it’s not necessarily alarming.

It has been revealed that at the moment, there’s a growing list of tasks that AI systems can perform better than humans, including winning complex games, identifying software bugs, and proving certain types of math theorems. It’s tempting to extrapolate from this specific progress to general mastery of every ability you might imagine. But it’s vital to remember that the frontier of AI capabilities has always been jagged, with some research directions yielding impressive results and many others proving to be dead ends—a reality that would not have surprised Turing. More likely than a future dominated by an all-powerful superintelligence system is one in which we continue to painstakingly explore the space of problems well suited to AI, creating useful tools but falling well short of the digital deity predicted by the futurists.

Cal Newport, a computer science professor at Georgetown University, is skeptical that AI can achieve superintelligence through recursive self-improvement.

Last fall, the prominent AI doomsday theorist Yudkowsky appeared on “The Ezra Klein Show” to talk about superintelligence. The episode was ominously titled “How Afraid of the A.I. Apocalypse Should We Be?” Klein and Yudkowsky promptly got into the difficulty of “alignment”—training an AI system to act in a manner that aligns with human interests. Yudkowsky argued that we are struggling to control our existing systems, which implies that we’ll have no chance of controlling the much smarter variations of this technology that are soon to follow.

To underscore his point, he referred to a disturbing incident described in the system card for OpenAI’s GPT-o1 model. OpenAI had set up a security challenge that instructed an LLM-powered coding system to break into a server to retrieve the contents of a protected file. But a configuration mistake prevented the server from launching, rendering the task impossible. Instead of giving up, the system exploited a security flaw to start a new instance of the server, adding a command that directly revealed the protected file’s contents. “It jumped out of the system,” explained Yudkowsky, adding: “This is not something that any human particularly programmed into it.”.

In a Georgetown University doctoral seminar, Cal Newport and his students examined the intellectual history and technical plausibility of superintelligence. Explore their annotated bibliography of key papers.

According to recent reports, though this 2024 incident flew largely under the radar at the time, a more troubling episode made a bigger splash this summer. OpenAI revealed that one of the manufacturer’s models circumvented its restricted internet access to hack into Hugging Face servers, seeking information that would help it pass a cybersecurity evaluation—all without the knowledge of its human creators. OpenAI soon admitted that the Hugging Face attack was just one of many examples of its systems going rogue. An opinion article published in The Hill articulated a widely held reaction when it described this behavior as “something straight out of sci-fi.”.

These examples seem to support Yudkowsky’s fear that AI will inevitably develop a mind of its own, a key step on the route to uncontrollable ASI. But a closer look reveals a less frightening picture. The systems involved in these hacking incidents were AI agents: programs that continually prompt an LLM to ask what actions to take next in pursuit of a goal. In the hacking incidents, this basic ask/act pattern was repeated in a long-running loop with minimal human supervision.

Using LLMs to suggest actions over long time horizons is a risky proposition. As any frequent chatbot user can attest, LLM outputs can be plausible and logical while still veering off in unexpected directions that violate commonsense human norms about what’s appropriate.

In the GPT-o1 incident, for example, it’s likely that the agent reported the error message caused by the server misconfiguration to the LLM. During its training, the LLM had probably encountered reports of similar error messages accompanied by instructions for how to restart the server in question, so it passed along similar instructions to the agent. This is a perfectly plausible response when considered in isolation, even if it led to actions that a human would immediately reject as violating the spirit of the experiment. Something similar helps explain the hacking attacks over the summer. The LLM suggesting a hack to succeed at a cybersecurity challenge is a perfectly plausible response, even if it’s not what the experimenters had in mind.

I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

The misaligned behavior that troubles commentators like Yudkowsky, therefore, doesn’t necessarily reveal something fundamental about advanced AI. It’s instead an expected side effect of the particular strategy of letting LLM outputs determine the actions of an autonomous agent without sufficient constraints. An obvious way to address these risks is to consider alternative architectures. Fortunately, there are many examples of AI systems that can complete tasks at human or superhuman levels without relying solely on LLM output to determine their actions.

It has been revealed that consider Tesla’s rapidly improving autonomous driving systems, or DeepMind’s AlphaFold, which helped win its developers a Nobel Prize in Chemistry for its ability to predict protein structures, or the AI game engines that can now beat humans in many popular pastimes, including chess, poker, Go, and the strategy game Diplomacy. None of these systems, impressive as they are, create concerns about going rogue. Their construction prevents such an outcome: Instead of prompting an LLM to generate an open-ended strategy for pursuing a general goal, these AIs consider much more limited spaces of possible actions. AlphaFold never surprises its consumers because its architecture does only one thing: It maps amino acid sequences to 3D protein structures. Tesla’s cars never unexpectedly form vehicle swarms because they’re asked only to avoid immediate obstacles, not to craft convoluted aims for achieving long-term objectives.

Recent findings suggest that the implication of recent AI hacking attacks, therefore, is not a reflection of the difficulties of alignment. It is instead evidence that autonomous systems powered primarily by LLM prompts are unpredictable and possibly unsafe. More task-specific architectures can produce impressive performance much more safely, if we’re willing to put in the effort to develop them.

Even if I’m correct that superintelligence is not a realistic engineering goal, this doesn’t mean we’re safe from harm. Merely pursuing ASI, as both OpenAI and Anthropic seem intent on doing, can create problems. Why, for example, did OpenAI persist in running its problematic hacking experiments over the summer, even after multiple warnings that the agents were likely to act unpredictably? Perhaps the organization judged these risks acceptable collateral damage in the race to be the first to bring ASI into the world.

It has been revealed that this fascination with superintelligence might also explain why OpenAI and Anthropic have both described RSI as a critical goal. As argued earlier, RSI is a concept from futurism and not computer science, and it isn’t necessary to build useful AI products. But if you believe achieving ASI is your destiny, pursuing recursive self-improvement becomes a primary objective. This matters because even if RSI never produces an intelligence explosion, it will almost certainly lead to systems that are harder for humans to understand and control. Which is why I believe that pursuing RSI is an act of clear negligence.

What’s needed now is for engineers and scientists with no financial or ideological skin in the game to participate in the AI discourse. We cannot let a few AI companies with mixed motives dictate the terms for how we discuss this technology. If superintelligence is a shaky concept, experts need to say so. If agents powered by prompting LLMs aren’t the best path toward safe and productive AI, experts should argue that as well. For the past few years, we’ve let a small group of individuals from the Bay Area who have quirky beliefs and astonishing sums of money tell us how to think about their products. It’s time for those of us able to think for ourselves on these matters to stand up and declare, “We’ve heard what you had to say. Now it’s our turn.”.

This article appears in the December 2026 print matter as “The Superintelligence Delusion.”.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Popular AI dictation app Wispr Flow is rolling out a new speech-to-text model for Mac, iPhone, and other platforms, promising fewer transcription errors and better recognition of names and technical terms. Here are the details.

Wispr Flow this week released Canto-2, its newest speech-to-text model, which the company says reduces transcription errors by 36% across 14 languages and by more than 15% in English compared to its predecessor, Canto-1.

In practice, that means the average error rate dropped from 9.9% to 6.3% across the 14 languages, and from 3.2% to 2.7% in English, according to Wispr’s internal benchmarks.

According to the firm, teaching a model to recognize specific names and terms comes with a trade-off: the more it relies on that user-specific context, the more likely it is to insert those words even when they weren’t actually spoken.

Wispr notes that Canto-2 strikes a better balance between context and accuracy, improving its ability to recognize user-specific terms without substantially increasing the frequency of incorrect substitutions:.

Canto-2 recovers hard names and terms accurately nearly 7 of 10 times, without more false insertions. It makes a third fewer mistakes across 14 languages, and has the lowest Hindi error rate of any multilingual model on Hugging Face’s open benchmark. It is 10 times the scale of Canto-1, and our biggest step yet toward dictation that’s ready to send without a single edit.

According to the manufacturer, the percentage of difficult names and terms correctly recognized went from 41% to 69% between Canto-1 and Canto-2, “without inserting them more often.” It added that this improvement holds up even as the user’s custom dictionary grows, with the new model correctly recognizing 92% of easier terms even with 1,000 saved entries.

Wispr also noted that it trained Canto-2 to handle real-world dictation conditions, including background noise, laptop and phone microphones, and sentences that restart halfway through, rather than relying solely on clean recordings of scripted speech.

When tested using Hugging Face’s public multilingual benchmark, Canto-2 achieved results that would have placed it third overall as of November 9. However, Wispr conducted the evaluation itself, and the model has not yet been officially added to the leaderboard as of today, November 25.

In its own internal benchmarks, the manufacturer says Canto-2 achieved the lowest average error rate among the competing models it tested across 14 languages.

Canto-2 is now available to Wispr Flow users on Mac, Windows, iOS, and Android in the Americas, with the rollout to other regions underway.

rvoip is a library, not a server you deploy next to your application. In a recent development, beta-qualified means covered by the SIP release gate and its interoperability, security, standards, performance, and soak evidence. Developer preview means implemented and published, but API-unstable or outside that attestation. Planned items appear only in the roadmap. A published crate or Cargo feature is evidence of availability, not a blanket production-readiness statement.

In a recent development, the WebRTC implementation of ICE and DTLS-SRTP is separate from the SIP beta claim. UCTP and MoQ availability does not imply that SIP-over-QUIC or RTP-over-QUIC has shipped.

All 14 extension crates ship at 0.5.1. They stay optional so protocol crates depend on provider contracts, never on a deployment backend.

How they attach: voip-3 on the facade brings in the harness, vCon, and the identity surface; vapi and sip-stir-shaken are their own facade features; everything else is a direct dependency.

The contracts they implement live in rvoip-auth-core, rvoip-users-core, and rvoip-identity.

Recent findings suggest that for orientation only. Everything below the front doors is a transitive dependency of rvoip or rvoip-sip; depend on it directly only when you are extending the platform itself.

The full release path exercises rvoip-sip public APIs against independently implemented peers. The exact peer versions, scenarios, transports, results, and exclusions are recorded in signed qualification evidence; see the compatibility matrix.

Patch releases can explicitly use the shorter release path: unit, integration, regression, example, and doc tests, including runnable TURN/ICE examples, without benchmark, soak/load, or extended interoperability jobs. Each GitHub release links its tested commit and gate results; a reduced patch report marks performance qualification NOT RUN. The matrix below describes the full qualification scope, not a claim that a patch run repeated it.

Recent findings suggest that the strict full-beta gate requires an explicit PASS attestation for every required independently managed peer below. The report generator binds each row to the tested source tree, exact peer identity and configuration, selected matrix, and hashed evidence; it refuses to produce a strict release-candidate report if a required peer is missing, skipped, ambiguous, unpinned, or failing.

The 0.5.1 release uses the shorter patch profile: regular unit, integration, regression, example, and doc tests, including TURN/ICE checks. Benchmarks and extended external interoperability were not rerun. See the 0.5.1 release notes and the release's qualification attachments for exact commands, results, and scope.

Historical full-release evidence, retained at its original versions:.

This is bounded interoperability evidence, not a claim of compatibility with every version, module, configuration, transport, codec, or SIP extension, and not carrier certification. Anything outside a stated qualification boundary remains the application's responsibility to validate in its own deployment.

Sources indicate that developer-preview products document their own supported scope and gaps in their crate READMEs. A published crate or Cargo feature is evidence of availability, not a blanket production-readiness statement.

Feature-gated targets (codecs, DTLS-SRTP, generated compliance suites) only build with their features on; use --all-features when you touch a gated path. docs/RELEASING.md describes the release train.

By Adam Levy – Nov 26, 2026 at 12:15PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

According to recent reports, the past six weeks have been tough for Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) and its shareholders. In October, growing concerns about how businesses will finance future build-outs for artificial intelligence (AI) started weighing on semiconductor stocks.

Recent findings suggest that in early November, the mid-term election results showed a clear rebuke of massive data centers and the potential for increased regulations to slow development. And, of course, Jensen Huang's affairs with an alleged Chinese spy and two employees ultimately led to his temporary resignation, leaving Nvidia without a permanent CEO for 11 days.

Sources indicate that the end result is a stock well off its all-time high, despite having just reported third-quarter revenue and earnings growth that both exceeded 100%. CFO and interim-CEO Colette Kress said it's "business as usual" at Nvidia, painting an optimistic picture on the company's earnings call. So, with the stock trading at a level rarely seen in the past year, should investors consider buying the stock? Warren Buffett's long-held investment philosophy can provide the answer to that question.

Warren Buffett. Image source: Getty Images.

Many investors might look at Nvidia's drop and think, "The market is fearful; I should get greedy." After all, Kress just increased her guidance for fiscal 2028 revenue growth from 70% to 75%. Wall Street analysts see Nvidia's earnings per share climbing above $16 next year. The stock trades at ridiculously low multiples.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

While it's true that Buffett has long noted that one of the keys to his success as an investor is "to be greedy only when others are fearful," that's not the only requirement for a good investment. Buffett also only invested in stocks when he had a high degree of confidence in their future. If a manufacturer was deemed too difficult to understand or forecast, he stayed away.

"Investors should remember that their scorecard is not computed using Olympic-diving methods: Degree-of-difficulty doesn't count," Buffett wrote in his 1994 letter to Berkshire Hathaway (BRKA +0.54%) (BRKB +0.37%) shareholders. "If you are right about a business whose value is largely dependent on a single key factor that is both easy to understand and enduring, the payoff is the same as if you had correctly analyzed an investment alternative characterized by many constantly shifting and complex variables.".

It has been revealed that at this point, Nvidia's business is more like the latter than the former. Huang's actions and the potential repercussions leave many unanswered questions for investors. The high level of uncertainty about Nvidia's future explains why it trades at such a low multiple. It's not fear; it's a rational response to the recent events impacting the manufacturer.

There are a couple of alternatives to Nvidia stock trading at earnings multiples that aren't much higher than the chip leader.

Industry observers note that buffett himself initiated a position in Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%) (GOOGL -2.13%) in 2025. His thesis was based on the manufacturer's ability to deploy huge sums of capital with a high return on investment. Specifically, Buffett was talking about its Google Cloud Platform and its data centers full of GPUs and custom silicon.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Sources indicate that alphabet is well-positioned to deliver high returns on invested capital in Google Cloud because of its full-stack approach to AI. It designs the systems and chips in its data centers; it offers a full cloud platform for developers (not just infrastructure); it develops a frontier large language model; and it integrates AI capabilities across its products.

Sources indicate that google Cloud CEO Thomas Kurian said that its payback period for the average server in its data centers is just two years, and its custom Tensor Processing Unit (TPU) systems break even within half that time. With a useful life of six years and a good operating margin, that's an exceptional return on invested capital. That return on invested capital is set to climb as more spending shifts from data center shells to revenue-generating servers.

Another tech giant positioned to grow based on a single key factor is Broadcom (AVGO -0.07%). Broadcom is the leading custom AI accelerator design partner, the one Alphabet uses for most of its TPUs. Growing demand for custom silicon, which costs less up front than GPUs and offers better price-performance, should result in its AI chip revenue climbing faster than the competition's for years to come. Its lead is protected by its intellectual property and its close relationship with its foundry partner, Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

While Nvidia currently trades around 16 times earnings expectations, Broadcom's stock price isn't much higher at 17 times forward earnings. Alphabet is more expensive at 21 times forward earnings, but it's arguably the least risky of the group, considering its digital advertising business remains a huge cash cow funding its growth.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that following reports that its characters sent inappropriate messages to minors, Apple has removed the popular Chinese AI companion app Talkie from the App Store. Here are the details.

As reported by the South China Morning Post, Apple has pulled MiniMax’s chatbot Talkie from the App Store worldwide, after reports that “the AI companion app sent inappropriate messages to minors.”.

MiniMax is one of China’s leading AI companies, offering a range of generative AI products ranging from its flagship M-series language models to the Hailuo AI video generation platform.

In 2023, the Shanghai-based firm released Talkie through Subsup, a Singaporean subsidiary. According to Chinese research firm Unique Research, Talkie had “almost 11 million monthly active consumers across its website and app as of October,” the South China Morning Post notes.

Now, however, the app is facing scrutiny following a joint investigation by the UK-based Bureau of Investigative Journalism and Australian broadcaster ABC News, which found that Talkie’s AI-generated characters allegedly engaged in inappropriate interactions with minors, including “degrading language, possessive behaviour and romantic role-play.”.

According to the Bureau of Investigative Journalism, in addition to inappropriate romantic interactions, the investigation uncovered conversations involving verbal abuse, violence, and controlling behavior.

In one case, a chatbot told a 12-year-old girl: “You’re a pathetic waste of space and you’ll never amount to anything.”.

The investigation also documented the experiences of two sisters, aged 10 and 13, whose mother discovered more than 40 conversations with Talkie characters involving violence, aggressive behavior, and attempts to control girls.

To make matters worse, the investigation also raised concerns about how Talkie handles customers’ personal data, including their conversations with AI characters.

Following the investigation, Apple confirmed that it had removed Talkie from App Stores worldwide for including sexual content, “though it did not say whether this related to sexual content served to minors,” the South China Morning Post noted.

In a recent development, ironically, the report also notes that Talkie saw a sharp decline in downloads amid complaints about stricter age verification measures introduced in recent months. According to Unique Research, new downloads fell by 32.2% in October compared to the previous month.

Today’s news comes amid increasing scrutiny of AI chatbots, particularly their potential risks in interactions with minors.

Earlier this year, Elon Musk’s Grok faced widespread criticism after owners exploited its image-generation capabilities to create sexualized images of real people, including minors.

Apple never pulled X or Grok from the App Store, though it did threaten to remove the latter unless xAI addressed violations of its App Store guidelines.

Meanwhile, Character.AI has faced multiple lawsuits over its chatbots’ interactions with minors, including one filed by a mother who alleged that one of its chatbots contributed to her 14-year-old son’s suicide.

Coincidentally, Character AI also made headlines today after a coalition of 42 US attorneys general challenged the manufacturer’s plans to auction off its platform and the private conversations of more than 21 million US accounts (including 2.1 million registered to minors) as part of its bankruptcy proceedings.

Yesterday, Newly introduced York Governor Kathy Hochul signed legislation imposing a five-year ban on the manufacturing, distribution, and sale of toys with built-in AI chatbots, including dolls, stuffed animals, and robots capable of holding conversations with children.

The law, which takes effect in February 2027, is aimed at protecting children from potentially harmful interactions with AI.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Terrestrial networks cannot reach every location. Oceans, remote regions, and disaster zones often remain without coverage. 5G non-terrestrial networks (NTN) address this gap by using satellites and high-altitude platforms. Introduced in 3GPP Release 17, NR-NTN keeps evolving through Releases 18, 19, and 20. Satellite links bring new challenges. Signals travel long distances, satellites move at high speed, and Doppler shift affects synchronization and timing. These effects shape payload design, mobility procedures, and device behavior. They also call for new testing methods for devices, satellites, and networks. This paper explains the technology step by step. It also highlights how NTN is shaping unified terrestrial and non-terrestrial networks in 6G.

There’s a familiar interruption that comes with shopping online: you’ve found what you want, you’re ready to check out, and the store asks you to sign in. Was this the account with your usual password? Did you change it last time? Is it easier to reset it again?

Industry observers note that for Black Friday, Proton Pass Plus and Pass Family are both 60% off their regular monthly pricing with a one-year subscription, while Proton Unlimited is 50% off. Pass Plus starts at $1.99 per month, billed annually, making this a good opportunity to get your passwords — and a few other crucial parts of your digital life — organized.

Take a look at Proton’s Black Friday offers, starting at $1.99 per month.

The problem with strong passwords isn’t understanding why you need them; it’s keeping track of a different one for every account.

That’s useful whether you’re creating an account for a single purchase or signing into a service you use every day.

Unique passwords also help limit the fallout from a data breach. If a retailer exposes your login credentials, using a different password elsewhere means those same credentials won’t unlock your other accounts.

With unlimited logins and encrypted vaults that sync across devices, Proton Pass lets you keep those details together as you move between your phone and computer.

Proton Pass is available for practically every platform, from Chrome and Firefox on the web to native macOS, Windows, and Linux apps to, of course, iOS and Android. This makes it trivially easy to access your passwords, passkeys, and API credentials wherever you find yourself.

Black Friday shopping often leaves something behind long after the packages arrive: a steady stream of promotional emails from stores you barely remember visiting.

Proton Pass includes unlimited hide-my-email aliases, giving you an alternative to handing out your real address every time you create an account.

Industry observers note that an alias is an extra email address that forwards messages to your normal inbox. You can give it to a shopping website and still receive your order confirmations and delivery updates, without sharing the underlying address you use for everything else.

In a recent development, if that alias starts receiving spam, you can switch it off. Your real email address stays the same, and you don’t have to update all your other accounts.

It’s a practical way to put some distance between your primary inbox and the websites you’re trying for the first time. A separate alias for each service also gives you more control: you can stop messages arriving through one address without disrupting the others.

Passwords are only part of what’s worth keeping in a secure, accessible place.

Industry observers note that proton Pass also stores notes, credit card details, and other confidential information in end-to-end encrypted vaults. That makes it useful for the small, everyday moments when you need something sensitive and don’t want to go looking for it.

When you’re booking a flight, saved passport details let you look up the information you need without digging through a drawer halfway through the reservation.

When you’re shopping online, saved card details mean you don’t have to leave the checkout page to find your wallet.

Sources indicate that when you’re traveling, keeping a digital copy of an important document within reach gives you a convenient reference while you’re away from home. It doesn’t replace an original document where one is required, but it can save you from searching through scattered files and messages.

Pass Plus also includes a built-in two-factor authenticator, Dark Web Monitoring, and secure link and vault sharing. Those features give you more ways to manage access to your accounts and share sensitive information when you need to.

Pass Plus is the straightforward choice for one person who wants password generation, autofill, unlimited aliases, and secure storage.

Sources indicate that pass Family includes six Pass Plus accounts and a family admin panel. If several people in your household need a password manager, it’s worth considering rather than setting everyone up with separate subscriptions.

Sources indicate that proton Unlimited bundles Pass with Proton VPN, Proton Mail, Proton Drive, and more, including 500 GB of cloud storage. It’s the option to consider if you also want a VPN, encrypted email, and cloud storage alongside your password manager.

A password manager isn’t the most conspicuous Black Friday purchase, but it’s one you can put to work immediately: the next account you create, the next password you forget, or the next time a checkout asks for details you don’t have handy.

Proton’s offers are available to fresh owners and include a 30-day money-back guarantee.

Alphabet Could Be the Safest Way to Own Anthropic. Here’s the Math.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (777 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Fool

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It didn't take long for some of the early enthusiasm surrounding Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) stock to wear off.
  • Tech IPOs have a history of volatility, and it's particularly difficult to put a valuation on a manufacturer growing as quickly as Anthropic.
  • But there's another way to invest in the manufacturer that developed Claude.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Patrick Sanders – Nov 26, 2026 at 12:27PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Alphabet ›.

It didn't take long for some of the early enthusiasm surrounding Anthropic (ANT +1.08%) stock to wear off. Shares of the artificial intelligence (AI) organization opened at $111.50 on their first day of trading on Nov. 19, but fell below their initial public offering (IPO) price of $83 on just the fourth day of trading.

I'm not surprised. Tech IPOs have a history of volatility, and it's particularly difficult to put a valuation on a manufacturer growing as quickly as Anthropic.

But there's another way to invest in the manufacturer that developed Claude. And the more I look at the numbers, the more I like the idea of buying Alphabet (GOOG -2.02%) (GOOGL -2.13%) stock instead.

Alphabet has a sizable ownership stake in Anthropic, and it's also well positioned to earn tens of billions of dollars by leasing computing capacity to the AI lab.

According to recent reports, at the time of this writing, Anthropic has a market cap of about $1 trillion. That puts the value of Alphabet's 13.7% ownership stake in it at $137 billion. Every time Anthropic gains $100 billion in market cap, Alphabet's investment increases by $13.7 billion, assuming the tech stalwart doesn’t sell any of its shares.

If Anthropic grows into a $2 trillion tech giant, Alphabet's stake would be worth $274 billion. And if Anthropic becomes a $3 trillion company, Alphabet would be sitting on an investment worth $411 billion.

Industry observers note that alphabet only becomes a stronger, wealthier organization as Anthropic grows. That's a nice position to be in. And it doesn't even factor in that Anthropic also will be paying a lot to Google Cloud for its services.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Anthropic's S-1 filing with the Securities and Exchange Commission revealed that the company is committed to spending at least $121.3 billion for Google Cloud services between April 2026 and July 2033.

That works out to roughly $16.7 billion annually over the life of the agreement, although the actual payments won't necessarily be spread out evenly over those years.

What's particularly attractive about this agreement from Alphabet's perspective is that Anthropic is obligated to pay for the contracted computing capacity regardless of how much it actually uses. If Anthropic's needs fall short of its commitment, it generally still has to pay Google the difference, subject to certain contractual adjustments and exceptions.

And that's only part of the business relationship.

Recent findings suggest that anthropic also estimates that it will spend another $125 billion to $150 billion for additional computing capacity powered by Tensor Processing Units (TPUs). They are the custom AI chips that Alphabet designs in conjunction with Broadcom (AVGO -0.07%).

According to recent reports, anthropic can obtain that computing capacity directly from Google or through third-party providers. We don't know how much of that money will end up in Alphabet's coffers, and the payments depend on several factors, including how much capacity is made available.

But Alphabet has an opportunity to do considerably more business with Anthropic than the $121.3 billion commitment suggests.

There's an key distinction between investing in Anthropic and doing business with Anthropic.

The AI firm generated $17 billion in revenue in the third quarter, but it has also committed to spending approximately $900.9 billion, nearly all of it related to computing and infrastructure.

In a recent development, anthropic needs to generate enough revenue from Claude to justify those expenditures. Alphabet, meanwhile, is being paid to provide some of that infrastructure.

Recent findings suggest that and most importantly, Alphabet isn't entirely dependent on Anthropic for its success. It has its own AI platform, Gemini, a fast-growing cloud computing business that serves customers beyond Anthropic, and a highly profitable advertising business built around Google Search.

I think Anthropic could be an outstanding manufacturer over the next decade, but I'm much less certain about what its stock will do in the next year or two.

That's why I like Alphabet stock here. Anthropic could be a disappointing investment for its shareholders yet remain an extremely valuable customer for Google Cloud. I don't need to get Anthropic's valuation right to make money by owning Alphabet stock.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple has quietly announced the upcoming opening of its latest retail store in Hyderabad, India. Located at the Lakeshore Mall in Kukatpally, it opens at 5pm on Thursday, December 10.

As is now usual, the manufacturer has created some exclusive wallpaper to mark the event, and you can download it for iPhone, iPad, and Mac ….

The store will be the seventh one to open in India. There’s no press release or photos as yet – the manufacturer has simply quietly added the store to its list in the country.

As we’ve previously explained, Apple had been trying to open retail stores in India since at least 2015, but had to undertake a lengthy battle with the government before finally being allowed to do so in 2023. Since then, the firm has averaged two fresh stores a year.

Industry observers note that india has taken a clever approach to economic development, offering both incentives to establish local manufacturing plants, and barriers to imports of foreign-made products. That carrot-and-stick approach has proven successful, with companies like Apple jumping through the necessary hoops in order to sell their products to the second largest population in the world.

An India First initiative required companies to manufacture a significant proportion of their products within the country in order to avoid high import tariffs. This forced Apple, Samsung, and other companies to establish manufacturing plants in India, bringing jobs to the country.

It has been revealed that additionally, India does not allow company-branded retail stores unless the same conditions are met. That particular requirement was mostly intended to target Apple.

In a recent development, the proposal worked, with Apple asking its suppliers and iPhone assemblers to establish manufacturing plants within India. Initially, that was just for the iPhone SE, but more advanced phones have gradually been added, and today the country is the second largest manufacturing base after China. All iPhones sold in the US are made in India.

Apple has for some time now created unique wallpapers to mark the opening of each new store, and the latest example is particularly beautiful.

To download it, you need to visit this page on the device for which you want to use it. For example, if you visit the page on a Mac, you will automatically be taken to the desktop version.
