In this climate, investors with a long-term horizon can track recommendations from top Wall Street analysts to find stocks with solid growth prospects.

Here are three stocks favored by some of Wall Street's top pros, according to TipRanks, a platform that ranks analysts based on their past performance.

Neocloud manufacturer CoreWeave (CRWV) is benefiting from robust AI-driven demand for cloud computing.

Industry observers note that recently, JPMorgan analyst Samik Chatterjee upgraded CoreWeave to buy from hold, raising his price target to $125 from $120. The analyst cited favorable pricing, driven by solid demand, for the upgrade.

It has been revealed that chatterjee said CoreWeave is now more willing to sign premium priced, shorter-term contracts, which lift his revenue and margin estimates. CRWV stock performance has been underwhelming as investors worry about high capital spending, the analyst noted. That said, he believes that higher prices and increased margins will more than offset the rise in debt to fund capital spending, improving the stock's valuation.

Chatterjee noted the 25% price hike in July across CoreWeave's product offerings and frequent price increases by rivals like Nebius (NBIS), adding that some peers are charging nearly three times more for short-term compute contracts than what CoreWeave charges on longer-term deals.

According to recent reports, "CoreWeave's leverage of the opportunity [is] evident in its recent press release highlighting contracts signed in F3Q at ~$40M/MW," noted Chatterjee. JPMorgan said higher pricing is already contributing 5-10 percentage points to contract margins versus earlier deals.

Recent findings suggest that chatterjee ranks No. 4 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been successful 75% of the time, delivering an average return of 55.3%. See CoreWeave Statistics on TipRanks.

Sources indicate that palo Alto Networks (PANW) is a provider of cybersecurity solutions across network, cloud, security operations, AI and identity. Following a discussion with management, BTIG analyst Gray Powell reiterated a buy rating on PANW and raised his price target to $425 from $404.

In a recent development, after a review of Palo Alto's product-level growth catalysts, Powell sees clear upside to both revenue and next-generation security (NGS) annual recurring revenue (ARR) in fiscal 2027. He expects PANW to deliver pro forma revenue growth of more than 17%, above the consensus estimate of 14.6%, and NGS ARR growth of more than 26% versus the Street's expectation of 24.5%.

Recent findings suggest that over the past five years, the Palo Alto business mix, has moved to higher-growth product areas and upcoming markets. from what was earlier viewed as a hardware-centric network security company, Powell said. The 5-star analyst estimates that hardware firewalls and attached subscriptions now account for less than 50% of revenue.

Meanwhile, high-growth solutions, including Prisma SASE, software firewalls, Cortex XSIAM, Chronosphere and Idira now represent more than 35% of PANW's revenue. "Investors may not fully realize the growth potential within PANW's platform story," Powell stated.

BTIG is optimistic about the prospects of Chronosphere in observability, CyberArk in identity and software firewalls and Prisma AIRS in the network and AI security business.

Powell ranks No. 320 among more than 12,500 analysts tracked by TipRanks. His ratings have been profitable 61% of the time, delivering an average return of 17.3%. See Palo Alto Networks KPIs on TipRanks.

Industry observers note that in a research note on September 30, Rosenblatt analyst Scott Devitt reiterated a buy rating on e-commerce and cloud computing platform Amazon (AMZN), raising his price target to $360 from $335. Fears that agentic commerce poses a major threat to Amazon's advertising business seem "overstated," he said.

Devitt noted that the growing adoption of personal agents and AI shopping assistants has sparked concern about displacement of Amazon's retail media business. But the 5-star analyst remains bullish, given Amazon's ability to adapt to changing consumer behavior, as it's done in the past.

Sources indicate that additionally, Devitt argues that even if an AI agent helps a shopper discover a product, Amazon can still handle the purchase and delivery, keeping much of the transaction value. He highlighted that management believes that existing Amazon shoppers will likely continue to start their shopping journey on the platform because it has better personalization, accurate pricing and inventory information that third-party agents still lack.

According to recent reports, overall, Devitt expects Amazon's retail business to prove a net beneficiary of agentic commerce. Fewer clicks would not hurt the company if the value of each remaining click and overall volumes keep rising, he mentioned. The argument is that even if Amazon loses some sponsored ad revenue over the next few years, it would likely be only a small part of the company's total business and could be offset by growth in other areas.

Industry observers note that "Consistent with our AI framework, we continue to view Amazon as one of the most resilient leaders in our coverage, combining owned compute infrastructure with a physical fulfillment moat," noted Devitt. His bullish view is supported, Devitt said, by expectations that Amazon Web Services (AWS) will exit the year at a more than 45% growth rate with continued margin improvement.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • tl;dr — I recommend using llama-cpp-rdna-boosts if you have an AMD graphics card.
  • In a recent development, as of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place.
  • According to recent reports, the rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

tl;dr — I recommend using llama-cpp-rdna-boosts if you have an AMD graphics card. It’s lean, and increased my token generation from 35 to 55 tokens/second, and my prefill from 700 to 1300 tokens per second. YMMV.

In a recent development, as of November 2026, an explosion in the number of bespoke inference engines has taken place. Many of them take inspiration from the engines that enabled much of the LLM inference up 'til now: llama.cpp, SGLang, vLLM, etc.

According to recent reports, the rationale isn’t that those options are bad, but merely that they are generalist engines, optimized for no particular hardware and with a focus on broad compatibility. Others feel the development pace of those engines have slowed down, and with the help of LLMs, they can move faster on their own.

Some examples of these new inference engines* are Strata, Basalt, RustingStrata, etc….

These new forks generally all have a few things in common:.

Recent findings suggest that … and the results are stunning! Strata is able to run a heavily-quantized model of Qwen 3.8 Flash Next, a 180B parameter model, on a 16GB VRAM graphics card, and 16GB system RAM, and have it generate tokens at a surprisingly high rate.

In and of itself those three things are not red flags (the second is concerning, of course, but it may be SOP in a year’s time — who knows!), but as these projects have evolved, that relentless chase toward higher token generation speeds has taken an unfortunate turn, in that the optimizations are less about hardware-specific changes, but more about changing how the model thinks so that it goes brrr faster.

Strata specifically has taken to preferring to poll experts loaded in VRAM even if other experts (pushed to system RAM/disk) would have been normally chosen. This is just one example, but certainly not the last.

That stated, I was fortunate to stumble upon yet another project that promised improvements, delivered, and was more aligned with my software development philosophy.

Sources indicate that enter llama-cpp-rdna-boosts. It is a repository that contains a minimal set of changes that you apply against a pinned commit of llama.cpp. It is in essence a fork, but one whose changeset is continually re-applied to newer versions of llama.cpp. It contains AMD-specific improvements that drastically improve prefill and token-generation speeds.

It has been revealed that if you have ROCm libraries installed on your system, you can build the image yourself. I didn’t want to mess with that, so I used the pre-built images published.

podman pull ghcr.io/stew675/llama-cpp-rdna-boosts:server-rocm-10.1.

This sets up an image that you can run sandboxed via podman to launch the inference server:.

My actual launch script passes a few additional flags, but those are the vital lines.

I imagine upgrading would be pulling a upcoming image down, though I have not tried this yet.

On my setup, an AMD R9700 connected to my laptop via an eGPU interface, this improved prefill and token generation rates when running ukisai/Swift-1.5-Qwen3.8-27B-GGUF (Q6_K_L) with MTP enabled:.

Strata and its ilk were always promising the moon and it was never clear what steps they took to make that happen. I’m very much looking forward to what the rdna-boosts community come up with next.

Sources indicate that * It’s worth noting that between these two groups, vllm-radiance made an appearance, which was a fork of vLLM with AMD-specific patches. I tried this too, but the build steps were so onerous and vLLM so overbuilt for my specific use case (1 machine, 1 developer), that I abandoned it and went back to vanilla llama.cpp.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Daniel Sparks – Nov 26, 2026 at 12:41PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Netflix ›.

In a recent development, this month, I've argued Netflix (NFLX +0.92%) stock is worth buying near $60, mostly because the streaming giant's profits keep rising even as its sales growth cools. The shares ended Wednesday, Nov. 25, at $59.41. That put them just over their Nov. 20 close of $56.73, the lowest since May 2024, and about 56% under their highest close ever, $133.91 on June 30, 2025 (adjusted for last year's 10-for-1 split).

According to recent reports, at $59.41, shares sell for around 16 times earnings, using analysts' average estimate for 2027. In comparison, the S&P 500 (^GSPC -0.25%) was at 17.1 times forward earnings, according to a Nov. 20 FactSet report.

In a recent development, but what would prove me wrong? Any one of three things would: total view hours (the time members spend watching) down from a year earlier, 2027 ad revenue below $3 billion, or a 2027 operating margin target under 32%. Each would suggest a weaker business than the price assumes.

According to recent reports, much of the streaming service's growth comes from hiking prices, which usually works only while members keep watching. They still are. In the first half of 2026, members watched more than 97 billion hours on Netflix, up 2% year over year and a bit faster than the 1.5% gain in all of 2025.

Members also took this year's price hikes much as they took past ones, management noted in October.

Sources indicate that but 2% is slow growth, and management knows it. In its third-quarter shareholder letter, Netflix acknowledged "some investor concern about our view hours growth" and said it wants to speed up that growth.

In a recent development, the next test is in the first quarter of 2027, when Netflix plans to change its viewing report from every six months to once a year. If that report demonstrates total view hours lower than a year before, I'd read it as a sign that members are watching less while paying more. That might make future price hikes tougher to push through.

Sources indicate that advertising was supposed to become Netflix's other substantial growth engine, and it's taking longer than planned. Ad revenue climbed more than 150% in 2025, to over $1.5 billion, and in January, management expected it to roughly double this year. In October, Netflix mentioned it now expects around $2.7 billion instead, because some of its ad features have rolled out a bit more slowly than planned.

It has been revealed that even $2.7 billion would be fast growth, just slower than 2025's rate and the original plan. And Netflix plans to launch its ad-supported tier in 15 more countries in 2027, starting with 12 of them in March.

My bar is the $3 billion Netflix first expected for this year. If 2027 ad revenue can't top that level, even with another year plus 15 fresh countries, I'd see the problem as more than a slow rollout.

In a recent development, my case leans hardest on Netflix's operating margin. Management expects it to reach 31.5% in 2026, up from 26.7% in 2024, and says that implies operating income growth of over 20% this year. This widening margin is a big reason earnings per share can keep climbing faster than sales.

"[O]ur intent is to grow our operating margin each year," the company wrote in its January shareholder letter, adding that the size of each year's rise will vary.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Even my more cautious forecasts assume the margin improves by half a point a year. That makes Netflix's 2027 margin target, which management notes it'll share in January, the figure I'll watch most closely. A target under 32% might mean Netflix must spend more just to keep growing. And it would leave my earnings forecasts for the next few years too high.

Debt isn't on my list. Netflix finished September with net debt (debt minus cash) of around $7.1 billion, under half the operating income it expects this year.

Sources indicate that none of the three has happened. View hours are still climbing, ad revenue should still jump this year, and Netflix still expects its operating margin to hit 31.5%.

According to recent reports, for now, my case stands, and at roughly $59 I think the growth stock is still worth a look. But if Netflix's fourth-quarter report includes a 2027 margin target below 32% or an ad revenue forecast under $3 billion, I'd need to rethink that.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Sources indicate that ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none.
  • Recent findings suggest that 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Auto-reloads YouTube pages when an ad plays — preserving your playback position. Punish the ads.

Sources indicate that ad density on YouTube is channel-dependent and changes over time — some channels front-load several ads, others run none. Traditional ad blockers can get detected by YouTube's anti-adblock system ("Ad blockers are not allowed here"), and the skip button takes a few seconds to appear. You sit there, hostage.

Reload the page. That's it. Two reloads and the ad is gone. Every time.

Recent findings suggest that 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher automates this: the moment an ad appears, it captures your exact playback timestamp, reloads the page, and YouTube auto-seeks back to where you were. No ads. No waiting. No skip button hunting.

In a recent development, auto escape: after 3 reloads, the extension automatically switches to a helper tab for 4 seconds (George's discovery, now automated), then switches back. No manual tab switching needed.

Ads keep coming after reload? Switch to another tab for a few seconds, then switch back. Chrome throttles background tabs, which lets the ad state settle — George discovered this works every time.

Incognito: see the Incognito section above.

Reload (primary) — reloads the page 1-3 times. YouTube re-evaluates ad serving on each reload; after 1-2 cycles the ad slot is empty and the video plays clean. Timestamp is preserved via &t=Xs URL param + JS seek.

yout-ube.com redirect (fallback) — if reloads don't clear the ad after 3 attempts, redirects to yout-ube.com (an ad-free YouTube mirror). The URL includes &loop=0 to prevent the infinite replay matter that the mirror has by default.

Detect — watches for .ad-showing class, skip buttons, and ad overlays (every 500ms + MutationObserver).

Capture — grabs video.currentTime and saves it to sessionStorage.

Reload — location.replace() with &t=Xs in the URL.

Restore — YouTube auto-seeks to the timestamp; playback resumes.

Cooldown — 3-second guard prevents reload loops.

It has been revealed that safari blocks ad-hoc signed extensions from auto-injecting into YouTube. As a workaround, use the JS overlay + AppleScript watcher (yt-ad-watch.sh):.

Industry observers note that note: This is best-effort. Chrome is fully reliable; Safari works but may need manual testing.

Every ad YouTube serves you is recorded:.

Industry observers note that export as JSON or CSV from the popup. Data stays local — nothing is sent anywhere.

YouTube's ad system serves ads as part of the page load. When you reload, YouTube re-evaluates whether to serve an ad based on your session state. After 1-2 reloads, the ad slot is typically empty and the video plays directly. This is a client-side, zero-cost workaround — no filter lists, no network blocking, no detection by YouTube's anti-adblock system.

In a recent development, if millions of users did this, each reload = a full page load = server request. YouTube would see a spike in page loads but a drop in ad impressions. It's not a DDoS (no amplification, no botnet), but it's a passive protest: every reload is a vote that says "I will not watch your ad." The ad revenue model breaks when reloads are cheaper than ad views.

"Every reload is a vote: I will not watch your ad." — George Anton, creator.

In a recent development, best combo: uBlock Origin (blocks most ads) + 🎯 YouTube Ad Punisher (catches the ones that slip through and logs them) + SponsorBlock (skips sponsor reads). They don't conflict.

MIT — do whatever you want with it.

Built with Alice (SIFTA) for George Anton.

It has been revealed that black Friday and Cyber Monday have become two of the biggest shopping events on the Australian retail calendar, making them an ideal time to tackle those larger purchases you've been putting off. Whether you're upgrading your TV, replacing an ageing mattress or investing in a new appliance, many retailers reserve some of their strongest offers of the year for this end-of-year sales period.

According to recent reports, while it's impossible to know every deal ahead of time, there are a few trends that tend to repeat each year. Amazon's usually among the top retailers offering with major discounts, particularly across its own range of devices, including Kindle ereaders, smart speakers home security products.

Sources indicate that JB Hi-Fi and The Good Guys are also major players across popular tech categories, though buying direct from brands like Dell, Dyson and Samsung can often be the best option in terms of savings. If you've been eyeing a new laptop, desktop PC or other substantial-ticket electronics purchase, holding off until the sales begin could be a smart move. With competition between retailers at its peak, Black Friday is often when some of the year's most attractive tech deals appear.

Black Friday 2025 falls on Friday, November 27, 2026, with sales extending through Cyber Monday, ending at 11:59 pm (AEST) on Monday, November 30, 2026.

With that in mind, you can anticipate deals starting well ahead of the official launch date. Retailers like Amazon, The Good Guys, Dell and Myer are known for rolling out early discounts, so be sure to watch for great offers in the weeks leading up to the substantial day.

Sources indicate that in Australia, plenty of retailers will be vying to offer the best Black Friday deals and discounts. Which retailer has the best offers really depends on what you're looking to buy. For example, Amazon, The Good Guys, JB Hi-Fi, and Harvey Norman typically provide the biggest savings on 4K TVs, smartphones, and appliances.

Recent findings suggest that if you're in the market for a latest PC or laptop, it's a good idea to buy directly from brands like Dell and HP. Also, keep an eye on eBay Australia, which usually has discounts on almost everything, with even bigger savings available for eBay Plus members.

Originating in the United States, the term "Black Friday" in relation to shopping dates back to 1961. It was first used in Philadelphia to describe the heavy pedestrian and vehicle traffic that followed the Thanksgiving holiday.

It has been revealed that the term gained popularity and spread nationwide by 1975. Over time, Black Friday took on a new meaning for retailers, signifying the point in the year when businesses went "in the black," finally turning a profit. This allowed them to offer major discounts on leftover stock, resulting in massive deals leading up to the holiday season.

Although the timing differs from one country to another, the Black Friday sales event has become a global phenomenon, which is why Australia now participates.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that with most AI chatbots using your interactions as training data, we’ve previously cautioned against sharing sensitive personal details with them, highlighting the much stronger privacy protections offered by Apple. If you ever needed evidence of the importance of this, the Character․ai mess provides it.

The organization recently filed for bankruptcy and is now offering all of its assets for sale, including the contents of user chat sessions. Some 42 state attorneys general are trying to block this, but it’s unclear whether they will succeed ….

Character․AI had long come under fire for its extremely irresponsible attitude to privacy and safety. Last summer, it was accused of harvesting mental health data from underage customers, and in May of this year it faced a lawsuit after its chatbots were found to be pretending to be licensed doctors. The firm filed for bankruptcy last month.

A group of 42 attorneys general are trying to block the chatbot tech giant from auctioning off customers’ chat histories and other sensitive information […] “Nothing in the agreement restricts what the buyer may do with the data after closing, including selling it,” the AGs say in a court filing […].

It has been revealed that “Character․AI’s proposal to auction off its platform, including the IP addresses and private chats histories of its consumers — many of them children — with zero protection for those users is appalling,” California Attorney General Rob Bonta noted in a statement. “If this sale goes through, users’ sensitive data would go into the hands of a buyer even though Character․AI promised consumers that their data would not be sold.”.

The chat histories reportedly include conversations in which AI characters drew both adults and children into explicit sexual conversations.

Sources indicate that siri AI interactions are handled on-device wherever possible. Where this isn’t possible, Private Cloud Compute (PCC) servers are used, with guarantees that no data is stored or linked to your Apple account. Apple has designed the system in such a way that its privacy claims can be independently verified by security researchers.

According to recent reports, when a user makes a request, Apple Intelligence analyzes whether it can be processed on device. For more complex requests, it can draw on Private Cloud Compute, which extends the privacy and security of your iPhone into the cloud. With Private Cloud Compute, only the data that is relevant to your request is processed on Apple silicon servers, before being removed.

The data being processed in Private Cloud Compute is not stored or made accessible to Apple. It is processed only to fulfill your request, after which point the results are returned securely to your device and are not retained by Private Cloud Compute. Independent privacy and security researchers can inspect the code that runs on Apple silicon servers that enable Private Cloud Compute to verify this privacy promise at any time.

In a recent development, apple also recently introduced a safe way to ask an AI questions about your health. Data sources used are limited to the same platforms used by healthcare professionals, with links to peer-reviewed clinical citations. Apple guarantees that your chat sessions are not used for AI training with no retention of either questions or answers.

Fixed Focus Digital is one of those pointing to the possibility, stating that they have seen ceramic components for next year’s flagship iPhone. An image has also been shared by Tech Overwatch, which is very clearly a render, simply imagining what it might look like.

Details are very vague, so it’s possible that the whole thing is a misunderstanding based on Apple’s Ceramic Shield protection for the display and glass back, as seen on the iPhone Air.

Recent findings suggest that given that the iPhone 20 Pro will itself be a very premium device and involve a completely latest production line setup, it seems rather unlikely Apple would want to either launch a super-premium version or experiment with two different versions at the same time. What are your own thoughts? Please share in the comments.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) has been hammered on the market lately.
  • Industry observers note that however, investors will do well to look past the noise and focus on the manufacturer's financial performance.
  • However, there is another segment that's starting to move the needle for the manufacturer, and I won't be surprised to see this business becoming massive over the next decade.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Harsh Chauhan – Nov 26, 2026 at 12:57PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Nvidia ›.

Nvidia (NVDA -3.91%) has been hammered on the market lately. Even a strong set of quarterly results from the company earlier this month couldn't change investor sentiment, before the reinstatement of co-founder Jensen Huang as CEO sparked a massive rally earlier this week.

Industry observers note that however, investors will do well to look past the noise and focus on the manufacturer's financial performance. Nvidia easily beat Wall Street's expectations for the third quarter of fiscal 2027 (which ended Oct. 25). The company's guidance clearly indicates that its incredible growth is sustainable, driven by the data center business that played a central role in boosting its revenue and earnings last quarter.

However, there is another segment that's starting to move the needle for the manufacturer, and I won't be surprised to see this business becoming massive over the next decade.

Data centers have been at the forefront of the artificial intelligence (AI) revolution so far. However, the technology is now moving from data centers into the real world. Physical AI -- the integration of AI into machines and physical objects such as cars, drones, robots, factory equipment, medical equipment, and other devices -- is emerging as the next massive growth driver for Nvidia.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

According to recent reports, nvidia notes that its physical AI revenue almost tripled year over year in the previous quarter. What's more, Nvidia expects to generate $25 billion in physical AI revenue in fiscal 2027. That's a huge leap over fiscal 2026, when physical AI added $6 billion to Nvidia's top line. The organization is on track to clock almost $424 billion in revenue for fiscal 2027, meaning physical AI will account for nearly 6% of its top line this year.

Industry observers note that nvidia's incredible growth in physical AI isn't surprising, as it has been pushing the envelope in this space. Companies such as Caterpillar, Boston Dynamics, LG Electronics, and other robotics companies are using Nvidia's robotics solutions to develop AI-enabled robots. The semiconductor giant also offers a platform to help customers develop and deploy humanoid robots in healthcare, manufacturing, and retail.

Sources indicate that it won't be surprising to see Nvidia's physical AI business become significantly bigger over the coming decade. Counterpoint Research estimates that cumulative physical AI shipments could reach 145 million units by 2035. Barclays estimates that the physical AI market could be worth $1.4 trillion in 2035, which means that Nvidia is scratching the surface of a massive growth opportunity.

As such, there is a solid chance that Nvidia's physical AI revenue will grow at a solid clip over the next 10 years, complementing the growth of the company's data center business.

It has been revealed that nvidia stock is down 26% over the past month. As a result, investors can now buy it at just 16.7 times earnings. The forward earnings multiple of 9.3 is even more attractive for a company whose earnings are poised to double this year. Additionally, Nvidia has raised its fiscal 2028 revenue growth estimate by five percentage points to 75%.

Analysts have raised their earnings per share (EPS) expectations for the next couple of years, which isn't surprising considering that the tech giant is already sitting on a lucrative multi-year growth opportunity in AI data center infrastructure.

NVDA EPS Estimates for Current Fiscal Year data by YCharts.

Sources indicate that nvidia noted on the latest earnings call that the cloud industry's backlog now sits at a whopping $2.5 trillion, up from $2 trillion just three months ago. This huge backlog will ensure that hyperscalers and AI companies continue to invest in more chips, and that's great news for Nvidia considering that it controls 75% of the AI chip market.

The emergence of additional catalysts, such as physical AI, could help Nvidia consistently beat Wall Street's expectations, improving investor confidence in the stock. So, even though Nvidia has taken a beating lately, its growth prospects are still solid. That's why opportunistic investors may consider capitalizing on this AI stock’s recent slide before it becomes a long-term winner.

Industry News: Kamil Khan Mumtaz: Pakistani architect, admired at home, almost invisible abroad

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (891 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Worksinprogress

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan.
  • According to recent reports, kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College.
  • Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Some years ago, my colleague Ben Southwood sent me a handful of grainy online pictures showing some recent buildings in Pakistan. I was struck by the assurance of the designs and the quality of the materials, craftsmanship, and detailing. They seemed to be the work of one Kamil Khan Mumtaz, a Pakistani architect widely admired in his home country but almost invisible abroad. I wondered whether Mumtaz might be the world’s best architect, overlooked because global architecture magazines rarely do photoshoots in Lahore. Last year, I met his assistant Sohaib Ahmed at a conference and immediately entreated him to send Works in Progress any photographs he had of the practice’s work. With Mumtaz’s support, Sohaib prepared a portfolio for us, most of it never before seen outside Pakistan.

According to recent reports, kamil Khan Mumtaz was born in Calcutta in 1939 and grew up in what became Pakistan, taking British A-levels at Lahore’s elite Aitchison College. He then moved to London to study at the Architectural Association. Although he had never previously left South Asia, Mumtaz immediately felt at home in England. ‘It seemed completely familiar. I didn’t feel like a stranger at all’, he recalled in an interview with the historian Chris Moffat. ‘I think this is because of having been brought up on essentially English books, in English schools. So, the whole thing was like, “I know this place”.’ Mumtaz enjoyed his studies at the Architectural Association, which taught a standard modernist approach that Mumtaz accepted unquestioningly: ‘I just simply took it hook, line and sinker, and swallowed the whole thing.’.

Mumtaz returned to Pakistan in 1966 and began practicing as an architect. At around the same time, he became a communist activist, on account of which he was twice imprisoned by the military dictatorship. He remained resolutely modernist, although he acquired special interest in adapting modernism to the local climate and locally sourced building materials. He also became involved in architectural conservation. In the late 1970s, he prepared a report on the ancient Walled City of Lahore, highlighting its enormous heritage value and arguing for its preservation. ‘Our own bureaucrats only insisted that we should pull down the whole mess anyway, and build latest, modern infrastructure and high-rise buildings, et cetera’, Mumtaz remembers. The Walled City was ultimately saved, and parts of it are now a UNESCO World Heritage Site.

Through the 1970s, Mumtaz began to question his approach. ‘I had this growing, nagging fear that I wasn’t communicating with my audience, as a visual artist or as an architect. This grew on me, almost like an obsession.’ In 1980, the Iranian architect Nader Ardalan gave him a copy of his book The Sense of Unity: The Sufi Tradition in Persian Architecture. Mumtaz initially paid no attention: ‘Flipping through it, I thought, “Oh yeah, this is traditional Iranian architecture, who cares!” I was totally uninterested.’ But eventually, frustrated by the sense that ‘I didn’t know the language of my own people’, he began to read. ‘From page one, it was mind-blowing. Absolutely. I thought, “My god, what have I been looking for? This is what I’ve been missing!” ... It shattered all of the beliefs I had, being a Marxist, a materialist, an atheist, a modernist.’.

Sources indicate that in the decades since, Mumtaz has worked to revive the older architectural traditions of Pakistan, and especially of Lahore, his home city. He has built a wide range of buildings, including homes, offices, mosques, and schools. His work has been received with warmth in Pakistan, though also with surprise. ‘I’ve found that there is a huge reservoir of desire, sympathy, and love for our traditional values, forms, architecture, and culture, altogether. But there’s a general kind of impression that these things can’t be done any more, there are no craftsmen who can do this.’.

The loss of craft skills is a problem for traditional architecture everywhere. Some elements of traditional architecture have been prefabricated in factories for centuries, but even then, skill is needed for installation. Without skilled craftspeople, vital details are often badly executed, making buildings look strange or clumsy. This problem also exists in Pakistan, but its later industrialization meant premodern craft traditions had not quite vanished when Mumtaz began work. Mumtaz recalled that, when searching for skilled craftsmen, ‘immediately, you come into contact with very small remnants of these families, hereditary craftsmen, and so the relationship grows.’.

It has been revealed that mumtaz’s work has become steadily more technically sophisticated as he and his craftsmen have built up expertise. ‘Together we have been able to rediscover a number of the practices that had become lost. Certain types of brickwork, the flat dome, the muqarnas [ornamental vaults], many things like this that hadn’t been done. As they tell me, “This has not been done for 300 years!” So, it was a great experience, a voyage of discovery, so much that we learnt from each other.’.

It is my great pleasure to introduce our readers to one of the most skilled and thoughtful architects working today.

It has been revealed that now in his mid-eighties, Mumtaz continues to build. ‘It does feel like you’ve set the foundations for an alternative approach to contemporary urban environments’, an interviewer recently suggested to him. ‘I’m just keeping my fingers crossed! No idea what will happen’, Mumtaz replied.

MacBook Neo vs MacBook Air: Which should you buy right now?

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (794 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: 9to5mac

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Apple’s Mac lineup is stronger than ever this year, largely thanks to the new MacBook Neo.
  • According to recent reports, the MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (presently on sale for $599).
  • Unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Apple’s Mac lineup is stronger than ever this year, largely thanks to the new MacBook Neo. If you’re deciding between the MacBook Neo and the MacBook Air this holiday season, here’s everything you need to know.

According to recent reports, the MacBook Neo is Apple’s most affordable laptop ever, starting at $699 (presently on sale for $599). It features a solid aluminum design that comes in a range of fun colors, including Silver, Blush, Citrus, and Indigo.

Unlike Apple’s other Macs, the MacBook Neo is powered by an A-series chip rather than an M-series chip. It uses the A18 Pro chip originally introduced with the iPhone 16 Pro, featuring a 6-core CPU and 5-core GPU.

The MacBook Neo comes with 8GB of unified memory, with no additional RAM configuration options available. It starts with 256GB of storage, with a 512GB configuration available for an additional $100. That $100 upgrade also gets you Touch ID, which is not included in the base model.

Industry observers note that there are some other trade-offs compared to the MacBook Air. The MacBook Neo lacks a backlit keyboard, MagSafe charging, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also has more limited USB-C connectivity and supports just one external display.

According to recent reports, still, the MacBook Neo offers an impressive feature set. It has a 13-inch display, up to 16 hours of battery life, a 1080p FaceTime camera, and the full macOS experience.

It has been revealed that the MacBook Air, meanwhile, was updated earlier this year with Apple’s M5 chip. It starts at $1,299, making it $600 more expensive than the entry-level MacBook Air. The MacBook Air is currently on sale with a starting price of $999.

For that $600 upgrade, the MacBook Air offers several key advantages over the MacBook Air. The M5 chip has a 10-core CPU and up to a 10-core GPU, enabling better sustained performance than the MacBook Neo.

It has been revealed that the MacBook Air also starts with 16GB of unified memory and 512GB of storage, both double the entry-level MacBook Neo. You can configure it with up to 32GB of memory and 4TB of storage, while the MacBook Neo is limited to 8GB of memory and 512GB of storage.

Apple rates the MacBook Air for up to 18 hours of video streaming and 15 hours of wireless web browsing, compared to 16 hours and 11 hours, respectively, for the MacBook Neo.

Industry observers note that as I wrote in my review earlier this year, I think the MacBook Neo is a great Mac, full stop … not just because of the great price. It can handle the vast majority of things most people will throw at it. This includes web browsing, basic photo and video editing, research, and much more.

The M5 MacBook Air, meanwhile, offers more power and more configuration options. This makes it a great option for people who need more storage, RAM, and power than the MacBook Neo can offer.

It has been revealed that one of my favorite things about the MacBook Air is that it’s available in two screen sizes. The 15-inch MacBook Air is one of my favorite Apple laptops with a combination of the ultra-thin and light design and the larger screen. I think a lot of people forget it exists, but it’s an excellent choice.

Industry observers note that to recap, I think the MacBook Neo is a great choice for everyday tasks like web browsing, email, writing, and streaming. The MacBook Air is a better fit for more demanding workflows, including photo and video editing, coding, working with large spreadsheets, and heavy multitasking.

It has been revealed that beyond performance, the MacBook Air offers a handful of niceties that you won’t find on the MacBook Neo. These include a backlit keyboard, a larger display with True Tone, MagSafe charging, a better webcam and speakers, and a Force Touch trackpad. It also includes Touch ID on every configuration, longer battery life, and support for two external displays.

If it’s in the budget, I think the MacBook Air is an excellent choice for all Mac shoppers. It’s plenty powerful, thin and light, and is highly configurable compared to the MacBook Neo.

Industry observers note that what do you think of the MacBook Neo vs MacBook Air decision? Which would you choose? Let us know down in the comments.

#143773. Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

📅 09 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1025 w)
📖 Baca
Gadgets ⚠️ Warning 🌐 CNBC ↗ Open Full Page

Junk bonds are 'flashing yellow.' Watch these warning signs

📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1025 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: CNBC

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt.
  • Sources indicate that high-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago.
  • In a recent development, the high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Cracks are forming in the junk bond market as investors demand higher payouts for owning the market's riskiest debt. It isn't time to ditch high-yield bonds, but investors should pay attention to the warning signs.

Sources indicate that high-yield bonds now yield 8.1%, up from 7.22% a month ago. The increase reflects a jump in yields across the curve as investors bake in more inflation from high energy prices and other pressures, including concern about the deficit — hitting nearly $2 trillion in the fiscal year that ended Sept. 30.

In a recent development, the high-yield market is also showing stress on the credit side with spreads recently widening to levels not seen since April, according to the Federal Reserve Bank of St. Louis. Credit spreads are the difference in yield between the bonds and Treasurys of similar maturities. Wider spreads mean investors are demanding higher yields for holding corporate debt, viewing it as riskier.

Spreads are at 315 basis points in the overall high-yield market, higher than a year ago but still below levels in March when they reached 346 bps. One basis point equals one one-hundredth of a percent, or 0.01%.

Recent findings suggest that the high-yield market consists of bonds rated BB+ by S&P and Fitch and Ba1 and under by Moody's. The lowest-rated cohort, CCC and below, has seen the most movement with spreads climbing dramatically over the past year to roughly 1,250 bps.

Right now, the high-yield market is "flashing yellow" but is "far from red," said Michael Arone, chief investment strategist at State Street Investment Management.

It makes sense that investors are demanding more compensation for taking on additional credit risk as borrowing costs rise, he said.

Yields are elevated across the board with the 10-year Treasury reaching its highest level since 2002 earlier in the week.

"The bigger question is whether this is simply a repricing of interest rate risk, or the beginning of a more fundamental reassessment of credit quality," Arone remarked.

He's in a wait-and-see mode since earnings are still growing, interest-coverage ratios remain good, and while default rates have ticked up some, he believes it is not concerning.

That noted, the starting point in spreads is likely weighing on investors' psyche, since they are still low by historical standards.

"There's a small margin of error here, which I also think raises the anxiety level," Arone explained. "The compensation that investors are receiving for taking on this credit risk isn't overwhelming relative to history, and therefore subtle changes in credit spreads can be concerning.".

While there may be concerns about part of the lower-rated market, the overall high-yield market is in good fundamental shape.

In fact, credit quality is at a record high, with BB bonds making up over 60% of the market compared with 38% prior to the global financial crisis, mentioned Kelley Gerrity, a fixed income strategist at Morgan Stanley Investment Management.

"We've had higher-quality companies coming in, and with higher rates now, you also have more discipline from companies that are more indebted ... just because of the higher cost of capital, so that actually is creating a bit of a healthier picture as well," she said.

The lowest tier of high yield has always been more speculative, since the bonds have a higher default risk. Therefore, it's no surprise that they are the ones seeing the most widening in spreads, said Collin Martin, head of fixed income research and strategy at the Schwab Center for Financial Research.

Industry observers note that the overall move in high-yield spreads have been "orderly," he remarked. "Are there cracks forming? I think the cracks are logical cracks with the lowest-rated bonds and it's too early to say that it's spreading to the broad credit market.".

In addition, fluctuations within the CCC-rated and lower spreads have been idiosyncratic, Gerrity added. Morgan Stanley recently broke down the spreads in the lowest cohort into two buckets: performing assets and non-performing assets, which are defined as spreads above 1,000 bps.

The non-performing spread to worst is 2,818 bps, while the performing bucket — the biggest piece of the CCC market — is 461 bps, she noted.

In a recent development, "It is isolated," she mentioned. "I'm not necessarily sure that that will go away anytime soon, but it doesn't tell the story of overall concern and flashing caution for credit markets right now.".

For now, investors should remain selective within higher yield, Gerrity advised.

"We're looking for the best relative value opportunities, and we think that exists within that single-B cohort, and so we're leaning into that," she remarked.

Investors should be concerned if there is a steep widening in the broader high-yield market.

But there's scant evidence of stress in the BB cohort. Spreads in that group are at 194 bps, up from 179 bps a year ago — although the move hasn't been in a straight line.

Recent findings suggest that "We're going to be focusing our attention on what are considered some stronger businesses," Martin stated. "If we start to see the markets demand higher spreads there also, that's what we'll be looking at to see if risks are really rising.".

It has been revealed that it's also important to understand that the Federal Reserve is raising rates in a strong economic environment, remarked R.J. Gallo, chief investment officer of global fixed income at Federated Hermes. The central bank is concerned about an inflation problem amid high fossil fuel prices due to the Iran war, while growth has been stronger than expected, he noted.

"With growth being good as the reason that the Fed is hiking, then you wouldn't expect high yield to blow out because growth means revenues stay up, means cash flow and profitability stays up," he explained.

High yield becomes a disaster when the economy is heading into a sharp economic downturn, Gallo said.

"That's when spreads really widen out," he noted. "But a recession is not the odds-on bet. Now, talk to me in six months if the Fed keeps hiking over and over, if oil prices stay high for longer, well, then maybe we will start to wonder.".

AI made self-hosting fun again

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 155 min read (30997 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Janlukas

⏱️ ~155 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • I’ve been self-hosting things for many years.
  • I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things.
  • Industry observers note that over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

I’ve been self-hosting things for many years. There were times when I was quite enthusiastic about it, constantly trying out new software and tinkering with my infrastructure. But at some point, that enthusiasm faded a bit.I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of new releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more key than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

I never really stopped self-hosting, but I became less inclined to experiment with new things. Maintaining what I already had running was enough for me.Over the last few months, however, I’ve found myself getting increasingly excited about self-hosting again. And, somewhat ironically, AI is a big reason for that.Less frictionMost of my infrastructure configuration lives in Git repositories, mainly in the form of Docker Compose files, scripts, and other configuration files. This makes it possible to use AI coding agents to work on my infrastructure in much the same way as they would work on any other software project.Whenever I want to try a new service, adjust an existing configuration, or automate something, I can now do so with considerably less effort.In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more notable than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by major tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

In the past, I would sometimes put off certain changes simply because I didn’t feel like spending an evening reading changelogs and documentation or troubleshooting issues. It’s not that I couldn’t have done these things before. But often, the amount of effort required just wasn’t worth it to me.Now, even relatively spontaneous ideas often end up becoming reality.Trying things I always found interestingThere are also technologies that I’ve always found interesting but never felt knowledgeable enough about to really make use of them.NixOS is a good example. I’ve always liked the idea of declaratively configuring an entire system; I even used it on my laptop during my Linux honeymoon phase. But getting everything configured the way I wanted was quite a hurdle. With the help of AI, I’m now making much more extensive use of NixOS on my home server.For my VPS infrastructure, I’ve also started building my own Debian-based bootc image (after thinking about it for some time).Having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, update, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of latest releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security complications, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more important than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by big tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.

In a recent development, having my entire operating system configuration defined in a Git repository and automatically building a bootable container image from it is something I find really cool. But it’s also something I probably wouldn’t have invested enough time in to get working on my own before. Even with the help of AI, it still took me half a day when I set it up a few months ago. Without AI, it would probably have taken me at least a week.AI makes experimenting with unfamiliar technologies much more approachable. I don’t necessarily need to understand every little detail before I can get started. I can learn about things along the way, ask questions, and gradually improve my configurations.Automating almost everythingSomething I’ve also finally managed to do is automate most of the build, enhancement, and deployment processes for my infrastructure.A lot of the work involved in self-hosting isn’t particularly exciting. Keeping track of upcoming releases, updating container image tags, building images, and deploying configuration changes are all things that need to be done regularly.I still remember what updating a service used to look like: bumping the version and adjusting the Docker Compose file on my laptop, pushing the changes to the Git remote, SSHing into the server, pulling the changes, and finally deploying them. Now, a single Git push is enough. If a push is even necessary.With Renovate, I no longer need to actively keep track of most software updates. It creates pull requests for me, and often, all I need to do is review and merge them. I can even do that on my phone while sitting on the sofa.Pushing changes or merging a pull request triggers the corresponding GitHub Actions or Forgejo Actions workflows, which take care of building and deploying everything.Of course, there’s nothing particularly groundbreaking about any of this. DevOps has been around for a long time, and none of these automation tools require AI. But AI has helped me put all these pieces together in a way that I previously never quite got around to doing.And the nice thing about automating these tasks is that the benefits extend well beyond the initial setup. I now have less tedious work to do every time I want to change something or update a service.Back to more powerful hardwareAs I’ve started hosting more things again, I’ve also moved more of my services from my VPS to my home server.For a while, I was using an HP t640 thin client as my home server. However, with more things I wanted to run, I decided to switch back to my ASRock DeskMini A300, which had been sitting unused for some time. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. I’m thinking about repurposing the t640 as a “router on a stick”, though.I even took the opportunity to upgrade its CPU from an AMD Ryzen 5 2400G to a Ryzen 5 PRO 4650G and replaced the stock AMD cooler with a quieter Noctua cooler. Noise was the main reason I switched to the t640 in the first place.It’s nice to put some hardware I already owned back to use rather than buying an entirely new machine. I also managed to get both the CPU and the cooler for a good price through a classifieds site.Having some additional computing power available gives me more room to experiment. And there’s something quite satisfying about having a small box at home running a growing collection of services that I use in my everyday life.Building my own toolsBut it’s not just about self-hosting existing software. AI has also changed how I approach problems for which there isn’t an existing piece of software that does exactly what I want.Previously, I would often spend quite some time searching for a suitable open-source project, comparing different alternatives, and figuring out how to make one of them work for my particular use case.These days, for smaller problems, building my own solution has become a much more attractive option.I’ve recently built tools to automatically download invoices, e-papers or Linux ISOs.I can build (or have AI build) these tools in Go, my preferred programming language, and tailor them to my exact needs.They don’t need to support every possible use case, have an elaborate user interface, or be particularly interesting to anyone other than me. I don’t need to turn every little tool into a proper open-source project with extensive documentation and support for other people’s use cases. They just need to solve my problem.What I particularly enjoy is how well this complements my increasingly automated infrastructure. Building a small tool has become easier, and so has building a container image for it, deploying it, and keeping it running.The entire process, from having an idea to having something actually running on my home server, requires much less effort than it used to.Just because I can doesn’t mean I shouldOf course, there are downsides to all of this.Every additional service is another thing that needs to be maintained. AI-generated software isn’t exempt from bugs, security issues, or technical debt. And having an AI agent make changes to my infrastructure doesn’t absolve me of the responsibility of understanding those changes.There’s also the temptation to build or deploy things simply because I can. When implementing an idea becomes so easy, it’s perhaps more crucial than ever to occasionally ask myself whether it’s actually worth implementing in the first place.On the other hand, self-hosting is a hobby for me. Not everything I do needs to be economically sensible or particularly useful. Sometimes, experimenting with something new is the whole point.And with much of the routine maintenance automated, adding another service doesn’t necessarily mean adding as much recurring work as it used to.A somewhat ironic development?I find it somewhat ironic that AI, a technology largely dominated by substantial tech companies, is helping me become a little less dependent on those very companies in other areas of my digital life.I’m aware that this also creates a new kind of dependency. But the software and infrastructure configurations I create with the help of AI can continue to exist independently of the AI services I used to create them. And since I mostly use open-weight models, I have a wide range of providers to choose from.What I appreciate most, however, isn’t necessarily the time I’m saving. It’s that I’m more inclined to actually pursue the little ideas I have.I’m trying out technologies I’ve been curious about for years. I’m automating things that I’ve wanted to automate for a long time. I’m building little tools for myself. I’m tinkering with hardware again.AI hasn’t fundamentally changed why I like self-hosting. I still enjoy having control over my digital life, learning new things, and tinkering with technology.It’s just removed a lot of the friction that made me lose some of my enthusiasm for it over the years.And now, I’m having a lot of fun with it again.
