  • According to recent reports, but I think Microsoft is being unfairly punished here.
  • Recent findings suggest that that's a major deal.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

By Patrick Sanders – Nov 26, 2026 at 5:00PM EST.

10 stocks we like better than Microsoft ›.

Industry observers note that tech stocks have been hit hard this month as investors worry about the enormous amount of money being spent on artificial intelligence (AI), and Microsoft (MSFT -1.25%) has been no exception. Shares are down about 13% from their all-time highs.

According to recent reports, but I think Microsoft is being unfairly punished here. While many big tech companies are free cash flow negative due to heavy AI spending, Microsoft has affirmed it will remain in the black at least through fiscal 2027.

Recent findings suggest that that's a major deal. And I think it's one reason why the tech sell-off in November presents an attractive buying opportunity for Microsoft before the end of 2026.

According to recent reports, microsoft is one of the biggest players in the cloud computing space, holding 21% of the global cloud infrastructure market. That makes Azure the second-largest provider of cloud services behind Amazon (AMZN -3.12%).

In Microsoft's fiscal first quarter of 2027, which ended Sept. 30, Azure revenue increased 48% from the previous year. Total Microsoft Cloud revenue was $63.9 billion, up 30% from a year ago, and the manufacturer's commercial backlog reached $677 billion.

That's an enormous amount of business coming down the line, so Microsoft is spending freely to ensure it has enough computing capacity to meet demand. It spent $45.2 billion on capex in the quarter. But even with that spending, free cash flow remained positive at $18.6 billion. That's because Microsoft generated $58 billion in operating cash flow during the quarter, up 29% from a year earlier.

That's a massive difference from some other tech companies whose AI spending has pushed free cash flow into negative territory.

NASDAQ · As of 4:00 PM ET 11/25/26.

Despite concerns about AI spending, Microsoft's underlying business is performing very well, thanks to its well-known software business. Nearly 4 million companies use Microsoft 365, including its popular office programs such as Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and Outlook.

It has been revealed that those subscriptions provide recurring revenue, while Microsoft's Copilot AI products provide opportunities to sell more services to existing customers. Microsoft 365 commercial cloud revenue increased 17% during the quarter.

That helped Microsoft's fiscal first-quarter revenue increase 19% to $92.3 billion, while operating income climbed 21% to $45.9 billion. Net income was $36.6 billion, up 32% from a year ago.

I don't expect Microsoft to slow its AI investments anytime soon -- and why should it? Microsoft Azure is generating substantial revenue, and Microsoft can continue to invest in the business while maintaining positive free cash flow.

Now down 13% from its all-time high, Microsoft offers investors an opportunity to buy a highly profitable firm with two powerful businesses -- cloud computing and productivity software. I think the market is overlooking Microsoft's ability to finance its AI ambitions, and it's an appealing opportunity for investors before year-end.

#143621. 4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

📅 25 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (733 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Nerdwallet ↗ Open Full Page

4 Ways to Prep Your Finances Before the Next Tech Outage

📅 25 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (733 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Nerdwallet

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.
  • Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year?
  • According to recent reports, but what about your money?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

If your social media feed is anything like mine, you’ve probably seen a reel or two on nonperishable food and solar-powered generators after the recent string of tech outages.

Have I considered giving water-filtering straws as stocking stuffers this year? Maybe.

According to recent reports, but what about your money? If your area was hit by a natural disaster or your bank had an outage, are your finances ready?

In a recent development, dan Stanush, senior financial planner at Charles Schwab in Asheville, North Carolina, recalls how fast financial conveniences disappeared after Hurricane Helene hit in 2024. “We lost power for three weeks and water for six weeks,” he said in an email. “And some local businesses could only accept cash or checks because card systems and ATMs were down.”.

Don’t get caught unprepared. Here are the moves experts suggest to help you weather various types of emergencies:.

Last week’s Chase outage was a good reminder that access to your bank balance can be disrupted. Stash at least enough cash at home — in small bills — to cover one week of expenses, claims Jeff Judge, a certified financial planner (CFP) with Chesapeake Financial Planners in Forest Hill, Maryland.

If systems go down, ATMs can go down with them, stated Eileen Olson, a CFP with Emerald Wealth in Daufuskie Island, South Carolina, in an email. Keeping cash in a safe at home is a good strategy, but it’s also smart to carry cash when you travel. (Remember when planes were grounded nationwide a week and a half ago?).

“My parents and sister were traveling overseas on 9/11 and got stuck much longer than they expected,” Olson mentioned. “After that, they always traveled with more cash.”.

According to recent reports, if your primary bank and its app were down, would you be able to pay bills? Having an account at more than one bank gives you an alternate funding source. Consider opening a high-yield savings account at a second bank or credit union for your emergency fund.

“This is the step I push hardest,” Judge notes. “I had a client whose debit card, credit card and savings all ran through one bank, so when that bank’s system went down, she couldn’t even buy gas.”.

If you don’t want to open a second bank account, a second credit card from a different bank and preferably on a different network (i.e. Visa vs. Mastercard) can provide another way to pay for things. “If there’s a problem with one credit card network, I have a backup with two other credit cards,” says Tony Steuer, author of “Get Ready! A Step-by-Step Planner for Maintaining Your Financial First Aid Kit.”.

Make a printed list of your accounts, along with account numbers and key contact numbers. Include your bank, insurers, credit card companies and any financial professionals. Store the list with copies of essential paperwork, including insurance policies and their declarations pages, estate planning documents, legal certificates and identification — potentially in a fire-resistant file box.

Keep a digital copy of your documents in a password-protected, encrypted spot as well. A password manager can store all of your login info.

Joon Um, a CFP with Secure Tax & Accounting in Beverly Hills, California, suggests digital storage site Everplans to his clients, but there are a variety of sites that offer encrypted document storage.

Take some time to write down how you’d pay for groceries, gas and medication if your usual payment methods weren’t available. What expenses would you need to cover first? What recurring bills are on autopay? Where would you keep the cash and any key documents you’d want to take with you if you had to leave home? Make sure other household members know where everything is.

And set a reminder to upgrade your records at regular intervals. Steuer, for instance, saves his account statements as PDFs and prints everything out once a year. “One of the massive concerns is that people could conceivably break into your 401(k) and drain your 401(k) account,” he states. Account statements could help if a hack affects any financial balances.

It all adds up to a web of protection that (hopefully) you’ll never have to use.

“The goal is not to anticipate every scenario,” noted Schwab's Dan Stanush, “but to have enough flexibility to meet basic needs while systems come back online.”.
